full_title: PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, PLAINTIFF-APPELLEE, VS. MARICRIS BAZAR Y BELLO, ACCUSED-APPELLANT.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: VIII. Evidence > D. Weight and Sufficiency (Rule 133) > 2. Direct and Circumstantial Evidence
topics: Requisites for conviction on circumstantial evidence; unbroken chain; test of moral certainty
Flight as evidence of guilt and its limits
Object evidence not linked to the accused or the victims; DNA results not formally offered
Court's power to order DNA testing motu proprio (Rule on DNA Evidence, Sec. 4)
Robbery with homicide; acquittal on reasonable doubt

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VIII. Constitutional Rights > M. Rights of the Accused

doctrine:
**Circumstantial evidence suffices to convict only if (a) there is more than one circumstance; (b) the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven; and (c) the combination of all the circumstances produces a conviction beyond reasonable doubt** (Rule 133, Rules of Court; reiterating People v. Modesto). The circumstances must form an unbroken chain leading to one fair and reasonable conclusion that points to the accused, to the exclusion of all others. **When the inculpatory facts can be explained in two or more ways, one of which is consistent with innocence, the evidence fails the test of moral certainty and cannot support a conviction.** Under People v. Monje, circumstantial evidence must be acted on with caution; all essential facts must be consistent with guilt; the facts must exclude every other theory; and they must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Because circumstantial evidence is only as strong as its weakest link, the prosecution must rely on the strength of its own case, not on the weakness of the defense.

**Flight per se does not establish guilt; it only tends to do so.** It must be coupled with other direct or circumstantial evidence, because it is inherently ambiguous and may have innocent explanations (fear of retribution, unwillingness to testify, fear of being wrongly apprehended). Flight that came only after the accused learned of a pursuit and a reward for her capture, after she had stayed beside the crime scene for hours, does not show a guilty conscience.

A blood-stained weapon and clothes found in a house occupied by about ten other people do not link the accused to the crime when no evidence traces the blood to the victims and nothing shows she wielded the weapon. DNA results that were not formally offered (and not recited in a stipulated testimony) cannot be considered. The Court observed that in a case resting purely on circumstantial evidence, the trial court could have ordered DNA testing **motu proprio** under Section 4 of the Rule on DNA Evidence, even if samples had already been tested at the police's request.
facts:
On the early morning of July 26, 2015, spouses Alexander and Septy Jane Oliveros left their house in Barangay Balintawak, Lipa City, for their market stall, leaving three grandchildren at home: Princess Shane (9), Prince Andrei (6), and Joyce Ann (6). Later that morning a nephew found the door open, the jalousie window broken and blood-stained, and the children dead in bed. They had died of traumatic head injuries with skull fractures. Septy Jane's wallet with PHP 40,000.00 and a bracelet worth PHP 55,000.00 were missing.

Maricris Bazar and Abegail Jaingue, both bar waitresses, rented a house next to the victims' house. Landlady Balbina Pelagio testified that about ten people lived there. When the police inspected the rented house, they found blood traces on a wall, blood-stained towels, a t-shirt, a curtain, and a coco lumber with bloody handprints. A request for DNA examination was made. At trial, however, the prosecution formally offered only the request, not the results, and the RTC did not admit it. The parties stipulated only that a police officer could identify the laboratory documents.

Maricris was charged with robbery with multiple homicide. She testified that she slept at the house that night, went out when neighbors screamed that children had been killed, left at around 9:00 a.m. for church with friends, returned, and then went to a birthday party. She did not go back because Abegail texted her that police were at the house and that a PHP 300,000.00 reward was offered for her apprehension, and because the barangay captain advised her to stay away. She stayed in Banay-Banay and later at her sister's house in Nasugbu, Batangas, until her arrest on March 9, 2016. Abegail testified that Maricris left at about 10:00 a.m., came back in the afternoon, and left her clothes behind, not scattered. Abegail herself stayed in the house for three more days.

The RTC acquitted Abegail because she was at work when the children died (around 2:30 a.m.). It convicted Maricris on six circumstances: her presence next door; the occupants' departure and the disarray of the house; her hurried departure without notice to the landlady and without her belongings; her never returning; her hiding until arrest; and the blood-stained items recovered from the house. It sentenced her to reclusion perpetua "without the possibility of parole" and ordered her to pay PHP 95,000.00 for the stolen property, plus civil indemnity and moral, exemplary, and temperate damages. The CA affirmed and corrected the crime's designation to robbery with homicide.
issues: Whether accused-appellant's presence in the house adjacent to the victims' house, and her leaving it without notice and without her belongings, point to her guilt.
Whether her flight and hiding until her arrest is evidence of guilt.
Whether the blood-stained coco lumber, towels, and clothes recovered from the rented house link her to the crime, and whether all the circumstances together prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
ruling:
**1. No.** The Court examined each circumstance and found that none excluded other explanations. *Presence next door:* both accused lived beside the victims, but so did about ten other occupants of the rented house. *Departure:* Septy Jane's own supplemental statement said that three unidentified men also left the house. Abegail's testimony, which the RTC found credible enough to acquit her, showed that Maricris left nearly eight hours after the killings, returned in the afternoon, and did not leave her clothes scattered. That testimony deserved more credence than Balbina's, since Balbina had no personal knowledge of when Maricris left.

**2. No.** Flight is "the evading of the course of justice by voluntarily withdrawing oneself in order to avoid arrest" (U.S. v. Alegado). Unexplained flight may tend to show guilt, but **"flight per se does not establish guilt but only tends to do so," cannot by itself overcome the presumption of innocence, and must be coupled with other evidence.** It is inherently ambiguous. As in People v. Bulawin, if the accused really meant to hide out of guilt, she would have fled at the first opportunity. Instead she stayed across from the crime scene for seven to eight hours and even returned. She fled only after learning of the reward for her capture and on the barangay captain's advice, so the adage that "the wicked man flees though no man pursueth" hardly applies.

**3. No, and the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.** The Information alleged that the children were killed with a coco lumber. But the prosecution offered only the requests for DNA examination, not the results, so the Court could not presume that the blood came from the victims. The exception to the formal-offer rule did not apply: although the documents were in the records and the parties stipulated that SPO4 Agustin could identify them, the stipulation did not recite their contents. The Court said the RTC "could have taken a more proactive role by ordering motu proprio the conduct of DNA testing" under Section 4 of the Rule on DNA Evidence. Earlier testing at the behest of the police did not preclude another test, since the information was relevant and would have dispelled doubts. Nothing showed that Maricris wielded the lumber, and with about ten other occupants, someone else could have used it, or used it against another person. Abegail did not notice any blood or blood-stained clothes during her three more days in the house, which leaves open the possibility that the items were placed there after Maricris left. It also "strains credulity" that a killer would bring the bloody weapon to her own room instead of leaving or disposing of it.

Citing U.S. v. Lim Sip (a crowbar found in a shared house did not prove guilt) and U.S. v. Villos (each link in the chain must be proven to the same certainty as the main fact), the Court held that **the inculpatory facts were capable of explanations consistent with innocence, so they did not meet the test of moral certainty.** "The accused is never called upon to disprove what the prosecution has not proved," and it is better to free a guilty person than to imprison one whose guilt has not been proved by the required quantum of evidence.
disposition: The appeal was GRANTED. The March 11, 2021 Decision of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 14046 was REVERSED and SET ASIDE. Maricris Bazar y Bello was ACQUITTED of robbery with homicide on reasonable doubt and ordered IMMEDIATELY RELEASED unless confined for another lawful cause. The Superintendent of the Correctional Institution for Women was directed to report the action taken within five days, and entry of judgment was ordered issued immediately.

bar_questions.q: Rico rented a room in a boarding house shared by about a dozen tenants, directly beside the house of an elderly couple. One night the couple were bludgeoned to death and their cash box was taken. Two days later, police searched the boarding house and found a blood-stained steel pipe in a common hallway near Rico's room. Rico had moved out the morning after the killing without telling the landlord. No witness saw the crime, no forensic evidence tied the blood on the pipe to the victims, and nothing showed Rico ever held the pipe. The RTC convicted Rico of robbery with homicide on these circumstances. Is the conviction proper?

alac.answer: No. The circumstantial evidence does not prove Rico's guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and he should be acquitted.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 133 of the Rules of Court, circumstantial evidence suffices to convict only if there is more than one circumstance, the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven, and the combination of all the circumstances produces a conviction beyond reasonable doubt. The circumstances must form an unbroken chain pointing to the accused to the exclusion of all others. Where the facts can be explained in two or more ways, one consistent with innocence, the test of moral certainty is not met. In People v. Bazar (G.R. No. 259037, September 29, 2025), the Court acquitted an accused convicted on her presence in a house next to the victims, her departure, her flight, and blood-stained items found in that house. About ten others lived there, and the blood was never traced to the victims.
alac.application: Each circumstance against Rico has an innocent explanation. Many tenants lived beside the victims. The pipe was found in a common hallway that any of a dozen tenants could reach, and nothing showed that the blood came from the victims or that Rico held the pipe. Moving out without notice to the landlord, standing alone, does not exclude other reasons. The chain does not point to Rico to the exclusion of all others. The prosecution cannot rely on the weakness of Rico's defense to fill these gaps.
alac.conclusion: The conviction is improper; Rico must be acquitted on reasonable doubt.

bar_questions.q: After a robbery-killing in their neighborhood, Lorna and Jun both left town. Lorna stayed in her house across the street from the crime scene for most of the day, talking with neighbors. She left only that evening, after a friend texted her that the police had named her a suspect and that a large reward was being offered for her capture. Jun, on the other hand, fled at dawn, minutes after the killing and before anyone knew of the crime, and gave no explanation. No other evidence links either of them to the crime. (a) May either be convicted on flight alone? (b) Does Lorna's flight have the same probative value as Jun's?

alac.answer: (a) No. Neither may be convicted on flight alone. (b) No. Lorna's flight, which was explained and came only after she learned she was being pursued, has little or no value as evidence of guilt, unlike Jun's unexplained flight before the crime was even known.
alac.legal_basis: Flight is the evading of the course of justice by voluntarily withdrawing oneself to avoid arrest or prosecution. Unexplained flight may be considered as tending to establish guilt, but flight per se does not establish guilt. It is insufficient to overcome the presumption of innocence and must be coupled with other evidence, because it is inherently ambiguous and may stem from innocent reasons such as fear of being wrongly apprehended. In People v. Bazar (G.R. No. 259037, September 29, 2025), the Court held that an accused who stayed near the crime scene for seven to eight hours and fled only after learning of a reward for her capture did not show a guilty conscience. Had she intended to hide out of guilt, she would have fled at the first opportunity.
alac.application: (a) Since no other evidence links Lorna or Jun to the crime, flight alone cannot support a conviction for either. (b) Lorna stayed for most of the day in plain view near the scene. She left only after learning she had been named a suspect and that a reward was offered, a situation in which fear of wrongful arrest is a natural explanation, as in Bazar. Jun's unexplained departure at the first opportunity, before the crime became known, is the kind of flight that may tend to show guilt. Even so, it would need corroborating evidence to convict.
alac.conclusion: Flight alone convicts neither, and Lorna's explained, post-pursuit flight carries far less weight than Jun's unexplained flight.

bar_questions.q: In a murder case resting purely on circumstantial evidence, police sent a blood-stained knife found in the accused's room to the crime laboratory, which issued a DNA report. At trial the prosecution formally offered only the letter-request for DNA examination, not the report. The parties stipulated that the laboratory officer "could identify" the report, but the stipulation said nothing about its findings. (a) May the court consider the DNA report in deciding the case? (b) What could the trial court itself have done to resolve the doubt about the source of the blood?

alac.answer: (a) No. The DNA report was not formally offered, and the exception to the formal-offer rule does not apply because its contents were never recited in the record. (b) The trial court could have ordered DNA testing motu proprio under Section 4 of the Rule on DNA Evidence.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 132 of the Rules of Court, the court considers only evidence that has been formally offered. In People v. Bazar (G.R. No. 259037, September 29, 2025), the Court refused to consider DNA laboratory results that were incorporated in the records and that a witness was stipulated to be able to identify, because "there was no recital of their contents, particularly the forensic findings, in the stipulated testimony"; the exception to the formal-offer rule therefore did not apply. The Court added that where the prosecution rests entirely on circumstantial evidence, the trial court may order DNA testing motu proprio under Section 4 of the Rule on DNA Evidence (A.M. No. 06-11-5-SC). Prior testing at the behest of police does not preclude another test for good reason, especially when the information is relevant to the proper resolution of the case.
alac.application: (a) Only the letter-request was offered. The stipulation that the officer could identify the report did not put its findings into evidence, so the court cannot presume that the blood on the knife came from the victim. (b) Because the case turned on circumstantial evidence and the source of the blood was decisive, the court could have ordered DNA testing on its own, even though the police had already had the knife tested. The results could have dispelled the doubt.
alac.conclusion: The unoffered DNA report cannot be considered, but the trial court could have ordered DNA testing motu proprio.

notes: Hernando, J., was Acting Chairperson (Special Order No. 3224, September 15, 2025); Gesmundo, C.J., was on official leave. The CA quote of Maricris's testimony gives the drinking spree as "July 25, 2016"; the year is evidently 2015 in context. The decision cites Sabay v. People for the exceptions to the formal-offer rule but does not state them. This digest states only what the decision says about why they did not apply.
